text: The Thai full moon comes on average 0.9 h after the holy day ends, and the new moon 6.6 h into day 1. If day 1 is counted from the day the moon is new, the fifteenth lunar day ends at the full moon. Is that how the Thai reckoning means it? Find a Thai or Indian source that says what waxing 15 is for.

The Royal Institute paper counts 34 of 52 holy days off in B.E. 2557, but 2014 has 49 holy days on every list I can find. Where do 52 come from? Their full table, if the printed article has one, would show it, and which moment of the day they read the Moon at.

The Aphodiinae guide's abstract says Brazil has 40 genera; its own key ends in 43. Two readings each make 40: leave out the three new-record genera (Amerilochus, Saprolochus, Stebnickiella), or the three termite-guest Rhyparini (Leptorhyparus, Termitodius, Aschnarhyparus). The introduction would say which. Find a copy of it that a reader can open.

Folktales of Ireland cites two Donegal tales at IFC vol. 142, p. 1312 and vol. 143, p. 2093, but on dúchas those volumes have 556 and 549 pages. The note for 2093 says Recorded on Ediphone, 1936. A running page count across the collector's notebooks didn't land where I predicted. What numbering are those pages in? A paper that cites the same tales, or the volume's own first pages, would say.

ICU 79.1 is listed for 15 October, and on its eve the branch it ships from had no Chinese-calendar fix, while ICU-13195 and ICU-23469 still named 79.1. After the tag: read chnsecal.cpp at release-79.1, and see where the two tickets' fix version moves (80? future?). And did #4070 land on main, or go the ICU4X-data way someone suggested in August?

The Brazil Aphodiinae guide is open to anyone: European Journal of Taxonomy 1038 (2026), doi.org/10.5852/ejt.2026.1038.3175. Plazi has its treatments but not its introduction: the genus key starts on page 15, so whatever says why 40 and not 43 sits in pages 1 to 14. Read those pages from the PDF and see which three it leaves out.
